prompt: What is the one difference between `while` and `do-while`?
hint: Same test, `n < 0`, gave two different outputs.

choices.text: When the condition is checked: before the body, or after it
choices.why: Right: so a `do-while` body runs at least once, and a `while` body maybe never.

choices.text: `do-while` counts, and `while` repeats until something becomes true
choices.why: Counting is what `for` says; both of these wait on a condition.

choices.text: `do-while` can only be left with `break`
choices.why: It ends when its condition is false, like `while`.

prompt: `for (int i = 0; i <= 3; i++)` — how many times does the body run?
`for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++)` — how many times is the test `i <= 3` evaluated?
hint: The last test is the one that fails.

prompt: Put the parts of `for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) { body }` in the order they first run.
The page loop ended with `5 days, -50 pages`. Why is `pages` negative?
hint: What did the last pass subtract, and what was left before it?

choices.text: An `int` overflowed after five subtractions
choices.why: 300 minus 350 is nowhere near the limits of an `int`; it is plain arithmetic.

choices.text: `while` runs one extra pass after the condition becomes false
choices.why: It stops at the first false test; the fifth pass ran because 50 pages were still left.

choices.text: The last day took 70 from the 50 left
choices.why: Right: the loop counts days correctly, and the leftover says by how much the last day was short.

prompt: `int i = 0; while (i < 10) { System.out.println(i); }` What happens, and what stops it at a terminal?

choices.text: It prints 0 to 9; nothing needs to stop it
choices.why: Nothing in the body changes `i`, so the test is true forever.

choices.text: It prints `0` forever, until `Ctrl+C`
choices.why: Right: the body never moves the condition towards `false`.

choices.text: The compiler refuses a loop whose condition never changes
choices.why: It compiled; the compiler does not try to prove a loop ends.

choices.text: The JVM stops it after one second with an error
choices.why: One second was `timeout`'s doing in the transcript; on its own it never ends.

prompt: How do you read the colon in `for (String t : titles)`?
hint: The section said it in one word.

choices.text: As "up to", like a range from `t` to the end
choices.why: There is no range in it; it hands over each element.

choices.text: As "in"
choices.why: Right: for each `String t` in `titles`.

choices.text: As "of type", since `titles` is the type of `t`
choices.why: The type of `t` is `String`, written before it; `titles` is the array being walked.

prompt: `for (int f : fines) { f = f * 2; }` left the array unchanged. Why?

choices.text: Arrays of `int` cannot be changed after they are created
choices.why: Their elements can be changed; the counting loop doubled them right after.

choices.text: `f` is a copy of each element
choices.why: Right: changing the copy never reaches the array.

choices.text: The multiplication happens after the loop ends
choices.why: It happens on every pass, to `f`.

choices.text: The compiler removed the line because its result is unused
choices.why: The compiler removes nothing here; the line ran and changed `f`.

prompt: Which of these jobs need the counting `for` rather than for-each? Choose all that apply.
hint: For-each to read, the counting `for` to write.

choices.text: Doubling every element of an `int[]` in place
choices.why: Yes: writing needs the position.

choices.text: Adding up the elements of an `int[]`
choices.why: Reading only; for-each does it with no position to get wrong.

choices.text: Printing `place 3 of 5` beside each title
choices.why: Yes: the position itself is printed.

choices.text: Printing every title in a `List<String>`
choices.why: For-each walks a `List` the same way it walks an array.

prompt: A for-each over a `List` works without any index. Where do the elements come from, according to the section?

choices.text: The compiler turns the `List` into an array first
choices.why: No array is made; the loop asks the collection for its elements one at a time.

choices.text: The loop asks the collection for its elements one at a time
choices.why: Right: through an `Iterator`, which lesson 34 shows.

choices.text: A hidden counter calls `get(i)` from 0 to `size()`
choices.why: That is one way to walk a list by hand; for-each asks the list itself, which works even for collections with no positions.

prompt: The loop `for (int n : stock)` is officially called the enhanced ___ loop.
In the years loop, what did `continue` do for 1899?
hint: The year was not printed, and the loop went on.

choices.text: Ended the loop
choices.why: That is `break`; 1928 and 1943 were still printed afterwards.

choices.text: Skipped to the next pass
choices.why: Right: the `println` below it was jumped over.

choices.text: Restarted the loop from the first year
choices.why: It moves on to the next element, never back to the first.

prompt: The plain `break` search printed `finished shelf 1` and `finished shelf 2` after finding the book. Why?

choices.text: `break` left only the inner loop, and the outer loop went on
choices.why: Right: it acts on the innermost loop around it.

choices.text: `break` inside an `if` leaves the `if`, not a loop
choices.why: `break` does not apply to `if`; it left the inner `for`.

choices.text: The book appears on three shelves
choices.why: It appears once, at 1/0; shelf 2 holds only `Macunaíma`.

choices.text: The JVM finishes every outer pass before honouring a `break`
choices.why: `break` takes effect at once; it just names the inner loop.

prompt: How do you leave both loops at once when the book is found?
hint: Give the outer loop a name.

choices.text: Write `break; break;` on two lines
choices.why: The first `break` leaves the inner loop and the second is never reached.

choices.text: Use `continue` in the inner loop instead of `break`
choices.why: `continue` moves on to the next place on the same shelf.

choices.text: Label the outer loop and `break` with the label
choices.why: Right: `search:` and then `break search`.

prompt: A label is a name followed by a ___, written immediately before a loop.
When does the section say a `while (true)` with a `break` inside is the honest shape?
hint: Where can the test be made?

choices.text: Whenever the loop should run at least once
choices.why: That is what `do-while` says, with its test in a visible place.

choices.text: Whenever the number of passes is unknown
choices.why: Then a plain `while` with the test in its header says it better.

choices.text: When the test is only possible in the middle of the body
choices.why: Right: after something is read or computed; otherwise put the test in the header.

hint: Counting, waiting, at least once, every element.

pairs.right: Counting a known number of passes
Repeating until a condition becomes false
Running the body at least once

prompt: `int[] a = new int[4];` Which loop writes the value 7 into every place?

choices.text: `for (int x : a) { x = 7; }`
choices.why: That changes a copy each time; the array stays all zeros.

choices.text: `for (int i = 1; i <= a.length; i++) { a[i] = 7; }`
choices.why: It skips 0 and then writes past the end, which throws.

choices.text: `for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { a[i] = 7; }`
choices.why: Right.

prompt: `int c = 0; while (true) { c++; if (c * 70 >= 300) { break; } }` What is `c` afterwards?

A loop that reads requests uses `while (running)`, and nothing inside the body ever sets `running` to `false`. It passed every test, which all stopped after ten requests. What goes wrong in production?
hint: What, inside the loop, moves the condition?

choices.text: It never ends
choices.why: Right: the tests stopped it from outside, which hid that nothing inside could.

choices.text: The JVM ends the loop when it runs out of requests
choices.why: The JVM ends nothing; the condition decides, and it never changes.

choices.text: It throws `StackOverflowError` after many passes
choices.why: A loop uses no new stack per pass; that error belongs to deep recursion.
